blocks.text: Matthew portrays several actors in the events leading to Jesus’ death: chief priests and elders press the case, crowds call for crucifixion, and Pilate makes the decision to hand Jesus over. The account therefore does not place its narrative agency on one group alone. Crucifixion remains a Roman state execution, even though Matthew also depicts Judean leaders and a crowd within the unfolding conflict. The darkness, torn temple curtain, earthquake, opened tombs, and the centurion’s confession are all part of Matthew’s narration of Jesus’ death; the guarded and sealed tomb closes the chapter with official concern about a possible claim of resurrection.

The mockery at the cross and Jesus’ cry of abandonment belong to a wider New Testament pattern of quoting and echoing the Psalms when speaking of Jesus’ suffering and resurrection. This makes these verses worth reading attentively as part of Matthew’s scriptural language, rather than as isolated details in the scene.

sections.title: Women at the Death and Burial

blocks.text: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary remain present as Jesus dies and is buried. Their presence links this chapter’s account of death and burial with the later empty-tomb and resurrection scenes, where they again witness events and are commissioned to report what they have seen.
